title: The Bank to the Studio Floor: Bethsabée de Rothschild, the Graham Technique, and the Founding of Israeli Modern Dance
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House at the Corner of the Concorde

stops.name: Paris, the bank passes to her father
stops.date_confidence: the marriage date of 1 March 1905 and the 1905 succession at de Rothschild Freres are attested by English Wikipedia; the regency of the Banque de France, 1906 to 1936, comes from French Wikipedia, which corrects the common description of the office as a directorship
stops.campa: On the first of March, Édouard Alphonse James de Rothschild marries Germaine Alice Halphen in Paris. His father Alphonse dies a few months later and the running of de Rothschild Frères passes to him; the following year he takes his father's chair as régent of the Banque de France, and the Hôtel de Saint-Florentin, bought by his grandfather James in 1838, passes to him with it. He will hold the regency for thirty years. The money that one day pays Israeli dancers is counted in this house.
suggested_refs: The banking house of de Rothschild Freres, Paris, inherited by Edouard Alphonse in 1905
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'
French Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'

stops.name: Baku, the oil fields sold to Royal Dutch Shell
stops.date_confidence: the year 1911 is attested by English Wikipedia; the month and day are not recorded, and the pin is the city rather than any named field
stops.campa: Édouard negotiates the sale of the family's Azerbaijan oil fields to Royal Dutch Shell. Wells worked by the Paris house for a generation pass out of Rothschild hands, and what comes back is a holding in the combine that is assembling the world's oil, and the Caspian is no longer a Rothschild concern. The sale is made three years before his fourth child is born. By the time she inherits, the Baku money is out of the ground and onto paper, which is the form it will travel in.
suggested_refs: The Rothschild Caspian oil holdings, sold to Royal Dutch Shell in 1911
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'

stops.name: Ferrieres, the brother who dies at five
stops.date_confidence: the death in 1911 of Edouard Alphonse Emile Lionel de Rothschild, born 1906, at the age of five, is attested by English Wikipedia; the place of death and the emergency operation come from French Wikipedia; no month or day is recorded, and the pin is the chateau at 48.8197, 2.7119, not the point 5.9 km east that earlier notes carried
stops.campa: At the château Joseph Paxton built for Baron James, modelled on Mentmore Towers, with a central hall a hundred and twenty feet long under a full glass skylight and a library of eight thousand volumes, the eldest son of the house is taken with appendicitis. Édouard Alphonse Émile Lionel de Rothschild, born in 1906, is operated on in an emergency at Ferrières and dies at five. His sister is not yet conceived. She is born three years later and grows up in the rooms he died in.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de Ferrieres, Seine-et-Marne, built by Joseph Paxton for Baron James de Rothschild
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'
French Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'

stops.name: London, the birth in the seventh week of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English and French Wikipedia; the address is unrecorded and the pin is the canonical London point used elsewhere in the atlas; no reachable source explains why the birth happens in England rather than Paris, and the wartime explanation carried in earlier notes is unsourced and has been struck
stops.campa: Bethsabée Louise Émilie Béatrice de Rothschild is born in London on the twenty-third of September, seven weeks into the war, fourth child of the baron and Germaine Halphen. No record says why the birth happens in England rather than in the Paris house. She is a great-granddaughter of James Mayer de Rothschild, who brought the family bank to France, and a granddaughter of Alphonse, whose Rembrandts and Islamic glass she will inherit and whose collection will be sold in this city eighty-six years from now.
suggested_refs: The birth register entry of 23 September 1914, London, not located in this pass

stops.name: Paris, the return to the Hotel de Saint-Florentin
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia places the family's relocation to Paris shortly after the September 1914 birth, and 1 January 1915 is an ordering anchor, not an attested date; earlier notes dated the return to 1918 or 1919 after the armistice, which the source does not support; the residence itself is attested by French Wikipedia, 'Hotel de Saint-Florentin'
stops.campa: The family carries the infant back to Paris, to the hôtel particulier at the corner of the Place de la Concorde where Talleyrand once lived and died. James de Rothschild bought it in 1838; Alphonse held it from 1857; Édouard has held it since 1906 and will live in it until the Germans come. Through its windows the child will watch the square that held the guillotine. The United States leases the house in 1948 and buys it outright in 1950, when the family that raised her no longer wants it.
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Saint-Florentin, 2 rue Saint-Florentin, Paris, Rothschild residence 1838 to the occupation

stops.name: Ferrieres, the childhood between two houses
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia attests the childhood divided between Ferrieres and the Paris residence and names the siblings; no year is given, and 1922 is an anchor inside the 1920s; the details of Jacqueline Piatigorsky's later life come from English Wikipedia, 'Jacqueline Piatigorsky'
stops.campa: Childhood divides between the Concorde and the château east of Paris: winter in the city, the estate in season, a girl moving between a banking house and a park laid out by Paxton. Her brother Guy will run the bank after their father. Her sister Jacqueline will marry the cellist Gregor Piatigorsky, settle in Los Angeles, play chess for the United States at the first Women's Olympiad, and die at a hundred. Bethsabée is the one who takes a degree in biology.
suggested_refs: Guy de Rothschild and Jacqueline de Rothschild Piatigorsky, her surviving siblings

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne degree in biology
stops.date_confidence: the biology degree at the Sorbonne is attested by English and French Wikipedia; the graduation year is given by no reachable source, and 1935 is the compiler's estimate from her age
stops.campa: She reads biology at the Sorbonne and takes her degree there. Daughters of the banking houses are educated for the salon; she is educated for the bench, and she is still at it when the war sends her across the Atlantic to Columbia. The laboratory holds her for a decade. Then she walks into a dance studio on Fifty-Seventh Street and does not go back to it. The foundation she endows in Israel thirty years later pays for arts and sciences out of one account.
suggested_refs: The Faculte des sciences of the University of Paris, where she took her biology degree

stops.name: Paris, the collection taken
stops.date_confidence: the confiscation of Edouard Alphonse's art collection during the occupation is attested by English Wikipedia; no month is given, and June 1940 is the entry of the German army into Paris, used here as an ordering anchor
stops.campa: The Germans enter Paris and the occupation authorities confiscate her father's art collection, the pictures and objects gathered by Alphonse and kept in the house on the rue Saint-Florentin. The family is already gone. What is looted here will be argued over for decades. What she carries out herself is small enough to wear: a jade necklace that a dancer in New York will notice on her chest six years from now and remember for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Rothschild confiscations of 1940 and the postwar restitution files
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'

stops.name: Lisbon, the road out of Europe
stops.date_confidence: the escape via Lisbon and the arrival in New York in 1940 are attested by English Wikipedia; the ship, the port of embarkation and the day are not recorded, and July 1940 is an ordering anchor
stops.campa: The French branch scatters to Britain, Spain, Portugal and the Americas as the front collapses. Bethsabée leaves with her parents by way of Lisbon, the last open door on the Atlantic, where the consulates and the shipping offices are the whole business of the city. The bank stays behind under German administration. The ship and the day are nowhere written down. What is written down is that the family reaches New York in 1940, and that she is twenty-five years old.
suggested_refs: The Lisbon transit route of 1940 and its consular paperwork
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'

stops.name: New York, the attestations
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia attests the refugee attestation work in New York without a date; October 1940 is an ordering anchor placing it after the arrival
stops.campa: In New York she goes to work on paper. Refugees arriving from Europe need attestations, affidavits of support and identity, before they can settle in the United States, and she spends the first American months obtaining them for people she does not know. She is twenty-six, a private person with no office of her own and a name that opens other people's, in a city filling with the newly stateless. Nobody has yet called her a patron of anything, and there is as yet nothing for her to be a patron of.
suggested_refs: The refugee affidavit apparatus of New York, 1940 to 1942

stops.name: Columbia University, the studies not finished
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia attests studies in chemistry, biochemistry and biology at Columbia without an advanced degree; no dates are given, and 1941 to 1942 is a reconstruction from the surrounding events
stops.campa: She enrols at Columbia in chemistry, biochemistry and biology, continuing the Sorbonne work in a second language. No advanced degree comes of it. The war takes her out of the laboratory, and when she returns to New York in peacetime she does not come back to Morningside Heights. The training stays. Every institution she founds in Israel afterward is built the way a laboratory is built, the teaching before the company and the running costs counted first.
suggested_refs: Columbia University registrar records for 1940 to 1942, not consulted in this pass

stops.name: New York, enlistment with the Free French
stops.date_confidence: the enlistment with the Free French in New York is attested by French Wikipedia; no year, bureau or address is given, and 1943 is an ordering anchor; earlier notes pinned this to Rockefeller Center at attested confidence, which their own annotation contradicted, so the pin here is the canonical New York point
stops.campa: She enlists with the Free French in New York, joining the exile apparatus enrolling French men and women abroad under de Gaulle. The daughter of the régent of the Banque de France puts on a uniform in a country that is in no danger of invasion, in order to go back toward one that has already been invaded. Her parents stay in America and will return to Paris only after the liberation. She goes first, and in uniform, and she is twenty-eight years old, with a degree in biology and no military training of any kind.
suggested_refs: The Free French delegation in New York and its enlistment registers

stops.name: London, the liaison officer
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia states only that she was posted to London as a liaison officer; no date is given, and September 1943 is an ordering anchor; earlier notes placed her at 4 Carlton Gardens at attested confidence while conceding the source does not name the building, so the pin here is the canonical London point
stops.campa: Posted to London, she serves as liaison officer between the French and American forces, work that consists of carrying orders and grievances between two armies that share an enemy and very little else. She is back in the city she was born in and has never lived in, twenty-nine years after the September she left it as an infant. She wears a French uniform in a British city, and the operation everyone in these offices is preparing for is on the coast of Normandy.
suggested_refs: The Free French headquarters at 4 Carlton Gardens, London, her probable but unattested place of work

stops.name: Normandy, the summer of the landings
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia places her in the landing force for the Battle of Normandy and the Batsheva company site says she participated in the Normandy invasion; NO SOURCE places her ashore on 6 June, and earlier notes dated this 1944-06-06 and framed it as D-Day, which is invented precision: women were not in the 6 June assault waves and Free French women such as the Rochambelles landed in August. The date carried here is summer 1944, exact day unrecorded; her unit is also unrecorded
stops.campa: She crosses to Normandy with the invasion force during the battle for the coast, one of a small number of women in French uniform to reach the beachhead that summer. The campaign runs from the sixth of June to the end of August, through the bocage and the closing of the Falaise pocket, and her part in it is recorded only as participation. She is twenty-nine. The country she left through Lisbon four years earlier is being taken back a hedgerow at a time, and she is inside it.
suggested_refs: The Rochambelles and the other French women's units landed in Normandy in August 1944
sources: Batsheva Dance Company official site, About

stops.name: Paris, the liberation
stops.date_confidence: August 1944 is attested by English and French Wikipedia for her liaison role during the liberation of Paris; no day is given, and the first of the month is the default
stops.campa: In August she is in Paris as liaison between the French and American armies during the liberation of the city. The Hôtel de Saint-Florentin stands on the Concorde with the family gone from it and the pictures gone from its walls. She comes back to the house of her childhood in the uniform of a country that had no government when she left, carrying a name the occupation had spent four years confiscating in every form it could reach. Her parents follow her home to France.
suggested_refs: The liberation of Paris, 19 to 25 August 1944, and the French liaison staffs attached to the American army

stops.name: Carnegie Hall Studio 61, New York: the school of Martha Graham
stops.date_confidence: the enrolment at Martha Graham's school after the war is attested by English and French Wikipedia; no year is given, and c. 1946 is reconstructed from Giora Manor's account, which places Robert Cohan's first sight of her after his demobilization; the Carnegie Hall pin is inherited from martha_graham.journey.json
stops.campa: Back in New York after demobilization she enrols at Martha Graham's school, a woman of thirty-one beginning a physical training most dancers start at eight. Graham has taught from Studio 61 in Carnegie Hall since 1926, building a technique out of contraction and release that nobody outside her own company is permitted to dance. Robert Cohan, one of her leading dancers, comes out of the men's dressing room after a class and notices a student wearing an enormous jade necklace.
stops.quote: As I came out of the boys' dressing room after a class, I noticed one of the girls emerging from the ladies' dressing room. What made me look closer was not her figure but rather a huge, beautiful jade necklace, which covered her chest. She noticed my interest and said, 'This jade is one of the few things I managed to save from our house in Paris when Hitler conquered France...' And I realized, this girl was not just any old Rothschild, but belonged to THE Rothschilds...
stops.quote_source: Robert Cohan, quoted in Giora Manor, 'Batsheva de Rothschild: Using Big Money for Modern Dance,' Machol Akhshav (Dance Today) no. 27, December 2014, p. 71
suggested_refs: Studio 61, Carnegie Hall, the Martha Graham school from 1926
sources: Giora Manor, Dance Today no. 27 (2014), p. 71

stops.name: New York, the cheque for a threatened season
stops.date_confidence: Giora Manor dates this only to 'one year in the late 1940s'; 1947 is an ordering anchor, not an attested year. The phrase 'one of the real Rothschilds' is Manor's own narratorial aside, not reported speech, and sits on p. 70 of the article, not p. 71 as earlier notes had it
stops.campa: Graham's New York season is short of money and about to be cancelled. Bethsabée takes out her chequebook in the office and writes for the sum required. From this year she is the company's principal patron: its operations, the filmed documentation of its repertory, and in time a permanent house to perform in. Modern dance in America has been made by women working without capital for twenty years. It acquires capital in a single afternoon, from a banking house that has just come back from four years of confiscation.
stops.quote: Batsheva simply took out her checquebook and wrote a cheque for the sum needed. She was, after all, 'one of the real Rothschilds'...
stops.quote_source: Giora Manor, 'Batsheva de Rothschild: Using Big Money for Modern Dance,' Machol Akhshav (Dance Today) no. 27, December 2014, p. 70
suggested_refs: The Martha Graham Dance Company seasons of the late 1940s and their private underwriting
sources: Giora Manor, Dance Today no. 27 (2014), p. 70
Batsheva Dance Company official site, About

stops.name: New York, the marriage to Donald Bloomingdale
stops.date_confidence: the 1948 marriage to Donald Bloomingdale, grandson of Lyman G. Bloomingdale, is attested by English Wikipedia; the place of the wedding is given by no source, and earlier notes placed it in Paris on the strength of an embassy posting that appears in neither Wikipedia. No source gives him any occupation. The New York pin is a default, not an attestation
stops.campa: She marries Donald Bloomingdale, grandson of Lyman G. Bloomingdale, co-founder of the department store. An American retail fortune and a European banking house meet in a wedding whose place no record gives and whose groom no record describes. He was born in 1913 and will die in 1954, at forty-one, and no source gives him an occupation. She keeps her own name through the marriage and after it, and the company she founds sixteen years from now is given that name rather than his.
suggested_refs: Donald Bloomingdale, 1913 to 1954, on whom the reachable record is nearly silent

stops.name: Paris, the death of the baron
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'
stops.campa: Baron Édouard Alphonse de Rothschild dies in Paris on the thirtieth of June, five years after coming home from America to a bank that had been run by the occupation and a house that had been emptied. He had held de Rothschild Frères since 1905 and the regency of the Banque de France for thirty years. His son Guy takes the bank. His daughter Bethsabée takes a share of the fortune and spends the next fifty years converting it into companies, foundations, studios and institutes.
suggested_refs: The estate of Edouard Alphonse de Rothschild, 1949
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Edouard Alphonse James de Rothschild'

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, New York: the room where dancers are rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: no source places de Rothschild herself in the Pilates studio; this stop marks the milieu her patronage sustains, and its date is an anchor inside the years of her Graham funding. The studio, its Graham and Balanchine traffic and the 1950 arrival of Carola Trier are attested in joseph_pilates.journey.json and its sources; the pin is inherited byte-identical from that file
stops.campa: Ten blocks from Carnegie Hall, in a building full of rehearsal floors, Joseph Pilates and his wife Clara run a boxers' gymnasium that has become the private clinic of American dance. Martha Graham sends her injured here. George Balanchine has been sending his since 1941. This year Carola Trier, a dancer who came out of a French internment camp, begins working on the floor. The apparatus is spring and carriage, built by hand. Twenty-five years from now she will endow an institute in the Negev to teach what is worked out in this room.
suggested_refs: The Body Conditioning Gym at 939 Eighth Avenue, Manhattan

stops.name: New York, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, LEFT OPEN: English Wikipedia gives the divorce as 1951; French Wikipedia writes that Bloomingdale was born 1913 and died 1954 and that she divorced him 'par la suite', which places the divorce after his death and is incoherent as written. 1951 is carried here as the English Wikipedia date, not as a resolution
stops.campa: The Bloomingdale marriage ends. She is thirty-six, without children, holding a Rothschild inheritance in a country not her own, four years into funding a dance company whose founder is fifty-seven and at the height of her powers. In the same year she goes to Israel for the first time. The two facts sit a few months apart in every account of her life, and no account of her life connects them. New York stays her address for another eleven years, and the Graham company stays her principal expenditure.
suggested_refs: The divorce record of Bethsabee de Rothschild and Donald Bloomingdale, not located in this pass

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the first sight of the country
stops.date_confidence: the first visit to Israel in 1951 is attested by English and French Wikipedia; no month is given, and June is an ordering anchor. Note that earlier summaries misread the English article as giving 1951 for immigration; it gives 1951 for a visit and 1962 for permanent settlement
stops.campa: She travels to Israel for the first time, to a state not yet three years old, absorbing refugees at a rate that is doubling its population and raising institutions faster than it can staff them. The country has dancers and no modern dance company, an audience for chamber music and no chamber music society, a music academy in Jerusalem with nobody in it teaching Graham technique. She is thirty-six, and what she does for a living is pay for a dance company in New York.
suggested_refs: Israel in 1951, in the middle of the mass immigration and austerity years

stops.name: Lod, the cameras at the airport
stops.date_confidence: the State Department tour and her role as assistant costumer are attested by French Wikipedia for 1956; the airport scene is Robert Cohan's recollection recorded by Giora Manor, who dates it only to the mid-1950s; no month or day is recorded
stops.campa: The Graham company tours the Far East on a State Department subsidy, with Bethsabée travelling as assistant costumer, and at every airport the press meets the plane and photographs Martha. At Lod, outside Tel Aviv, the photographers work out who the other woman is and do not stop. She has been the anonymous patron in the wings across a whole continent. In this country her name arrives ahead of her, and Robert Cohan, watching from the company, thinks she registers the difference.
stops.quote: At each airport we would disembark at, we were met by a posse of press photographers. And Martha would always present Bethsabee as Ms. De Rothschild. The reporters would look at Bethsabee for two seconds and concentrate on Martha again. But when we finally landed at the Tel Aviv airport at Lod, when they realized they were in front of a genuine Rothschild the cameras kept clicking. Perhaps Bethsabee also registered the difference. She realized that her name was a name to conjure with in Israel...
stops.quote_source: Robert Cohan, quoted in Giora Manor, 'Batsheva de Rothschild: Using Big Money for Modern Dance,' Machol Akhshav (Dance Today) no. 27, December 2014, p. 70
suggested_refs: Lod airport, arrival point of the 1956 Graham company tour
sources: Giora Manor, Dance Today no. 27 (2014), p. 70

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the tour extended at her own expense
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia attests that she paid personally to extend the State Department itinerary to Israel in 1956; the venue is named by no source, and earlier notes supplied the Habima Theatre as 'the era's principal stage', which is a reconstruction and is not carried; the pin is the city, and the month is an anchor
stops.campa: The State Department itinerary does not include Israel. She pays for the extension out of her own pocket and the Graham company dances in Tel Aviv, the first American modern dance the country sees performed live. She is not on the programme. She is in the wardrobe, handing out costumes. Eight years from now the company she founds in this city will begin its existence with this repertory already in its body and this technique already in its training.
suggested_refs: The 1956 Martha Graham performances in Israel, venue unrecorded in the reachable sources

stops.name: Jerusalem, the first Graham summer course
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia attests the first Martha Graham summer course at the Jerusalem music academy in 1958; no month is given. LOCATION CORRECTED: earlier notes pinned this to the Givat Ram campus, where the academy did not yet stand. Per English Wikipedia the school was on Hillel Street and in 1958 moved to a Smolenskin Street building in Rehavia bought with Samuel Rubin's money, taking the name Rubin Academy; the pin is central Jerusalem and is approximate
stops.campa: She establishes the first Martha Graham summer course at the Jerusalem music academy, which has just moved from Hillel Street into a Rehavia building bought with Samuel Rubin's money and taken the name Rubin Academy. Israeli dancers learn the contraction on Smolenskin Street in the summer heat. There is as yet no company for them to join. The training is in place six years before the institution that will need it. She is forty-three, and pays for the course herself.
suggested_refs: The Rubin Academy of Music, Rehavia, Jerusalem, from 1958
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Jerusalem Academy of Music and Dance'

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the name Batsheva and the foundation
stops.date_confidence: permanent settlement in Israel and the adoption of the Hebrew name in 1962 are attested by English and French Wikipedia. CONTRADICTION, LEFT OPEN: the Batsheva Dance Company's own site says she moved to Israel in 1956. The foundation is dated 1962 by French Wikipedia, which names Francois Shapira as its director; earlier notes dated two foundations to 1965 with no source, and described their remit as science and technology rather than arts and sciences
stops.campa: She settles in Israel for good and takes the Hebrew form of her name. Bethsabée becomes Batsheva, a French birth certificate rendered back into the language it came out of. The same year she endows the Fondation Batsheva de Rothschild under François Shapira, which buys music libraries and pays for the translation of ancient Hebrew texts; in Israel it is called the Batsheva de Rothschild Foundation for Arts and Sciences. The foundation, and the company she starts two years from now, are given the name she has just changed to.
suggested_refs: The Batsheva de Rothschild Foundation for Arts and Sciences, 1962
sources: Batsheva Dance Company official site, About

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the founding on Christmas Eve
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English Wikipedia; the pin is inherited byte-identical from martha_graham.journey.json, where this founding already stands as a stop
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve she founds a dance company in Tel Aviv and gives it her own name. Martha Graham is its artistic adviser; Batsheva de Rothschild is its chief executive and its entire endowment. Graham is seventy and has never lived in the country whose dancers now begin from her syllabus. The state is sixteen years old. Israeli modern dance begins on this date, as an American technique installed whole by a woman born in London to a Paris banking house.
suggested_refs: The founding charter of the Batsheva Dance Company, 24 December 1964

stops.name: Tel Aviv, seven works and one made new
stops.date_confidence: the seven donated works, the single new commission and the licensing of the repertory are attested by English Wikipedia without dates beyond the founding year; 1 January 1965 is an ordering anchor
stops.campa: Graham hands the young company seven of her existing works outright and choreographs one piece for it alone. The Batsheva dancers become the first performers anywhere outside her own company licensed to dance her repertory, a permission she has withheld from everybody for forty years. Merce Cunningham danced in that company through the war and left it to make a vocabulary of his own. The technique he walked away from is exported entire to Tel Aviv, on a patron's money, twenty years after he went.
suggested_refs: The seven Graham works ceded to Batsheva in 1964 and the one commissioned for it

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Jeannette Ordman comes from London
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 1965 as the year Ordman came to Israel from London and dates the meeting only to 'the mid-1960s'; these are two distinct facts and earlier notes collapsed them into one. The month is an anchor
stops.campa: Jeannette Ordman, a classical dancer born in South Africa and trained in London, arrives in Israel. She and Batsheva de Rothschild meet in these middle years of the decade. The meeting produces a school and a second company within three years, and in ten years it ends Batsheva's relationship with Martha Graham. Ordman will be the leading dancer of everything the two of them build together, and de Rothschild will fund her without interruption until the day she dies.
suggested_refs: Jeannette Ordman, 1935 to 2007, dancer and artistic director

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the Bat-Dor studios
stops.date_confidence: the founding of the Bat-Dor studios with Ordman in 1967 is attested by French Wikipedia; no month is given
stops.campa: She founds the Bat-Dor studios with Ordman: a school with a building and a floor of its own. Batsheva the company is three years old and full of Graham repertory. Bat-Dor is classical at its base and will take work from Alvin Ailey and Hans van Manen alongside Israeli choreographers. She is now funding two institutions in one city out of one fortune, one of them run by the woman she has chosen and the other by the technique she imported. The arrangement holds for eight years.
suggested_refs: The Bat-Dor studios, Tel Aviv, founded 1967

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the Bat-Dor company debuts
stops.date_confidence: the 1968 debut with Ordman as leading dancer and artistic director is attested by English Wikipedia; no month is given
stops.campa: The Bat-Dor Dance Company gives its first performances with Jeannette Ordman as leading dancer and artistic director. Israel now has two modern dance companies within four years of having none, both of them paid for out of the same account. Bat-Dor buys its repertory abroad and makes the rest at home, on her account and no one else's. The arrangement provides for no second patron. She is fifty-three, and the company will last thirty-eight years and outlive her by seven.
suggested_refs: The Bat-Dor Dance Company, Tel Aviv, 1968 to 2006
sources: English and French Wikipedia, 'Bethsabee de Rothschild'

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Jerome Robbins stages Moves
stops.date_confidence: Giora Manor dates the Robbins interview to the staging of Moves for Batsheva and the pool assigns it 1969; the month is not recorded and the year rests on Manor's article alone
stops.campa: Jerome Robbins comes from New York to set Moves on the Batsheva dancers, a ballet performed in silence, with no music of any kind. He tells an Israeli critic afterward that the companies he works with are usually terrified of him and that this one is not. Robbins is fifty and has West Side Story behind him. Five years after its founding, a company assembled out of a chequebook and a borrowed syllabus is taking choreographers who could work anywhere.
stops.quote: Usually the companies I work with are terrified of me; not the Batsheva dancers, of whom I am afraid…
stops.quote_source: Jerome Robbins, interviewed by Giora Manor when he came to stage Moves for Batsheva, Machol Akhshav (Dance Today) no. 27, December 2014, p. 67
suggested_refs: Jerome Robbins's Moves, staged for the Batsheva Dance Company
sources: Giora Manor, Dance Today no. 27 (2014), p. 67

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the argument in her office
stops.date_confidence: Manor dates the confrontation to 1973 and states that he is recounting it from memory some forty years later; no month or day is given, and the exchange survives in his account alone
stops.campa: The critic Giora Manor writes that she has no right to put an end to the company she founded. She summons him to her office and asks him how he could write it. He answers with a child, and a killing, and the police who would come for her. She does not concede the point. Manor will set the exchange down from memory forty years later, in the last thing he writes. The company is nine years old and she has been asked in print, for the first time, whether a founder owns what she founded.
stops.quote: How could you write I had no right to terminate the existence of the company I had founded and am financing?
stops.quote_source: Bethsabee de Rothschild to Giora Manor in her Tel Aviv office, 1973, quoted in Machol Akhshav (Dance Today) no. 27, December 2014, pp. 65-66
suggested_refs: Giora Manor's posthumous chapter on Batsheva de Rothschild, edited by Ruth Eshel
sources: Giora Manor, Dance Today no. 27 (2014), pp. 65-66

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Ordman made artistic director of Batsheva
stops.date_confidence: the 1974 appointment is attested by English Wikipedia; no month is given
stops.campa: She appoints Jeannette Ordman artistic director of Batsheva. A company trained in Graham technique is handed to a classically trained director from the other institution, and the dancers object; the objections travel to New York, to Martha Graham herself. The two companies she has funded separately for six years are being brought under a single hand, and it is the hand that has never belonged to the Graham line. Eighteen months later she stops paying for the company.
suggested_refs: The 1974 leadership crisis at the Batsheva Dance Company

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the funding withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: 1975 is attested by English Wikipedia and by the Batsheva company's own site; no month is given. CONTRADICTION OF CAUSE, LEFT OPEN: English Wikipedia gives the dancers' complaints to Graham about Ordman as the trigger, while the company's own site says that when plans to consolidate Batsheva with Bat-Dor failed she ceased supporting Batsheva. Both are carried; neither is preferred
stops.campa: She stops paying for Batsheva. The company's own account says a plan to merge it with Bat-Dor has failed. The English record says the dancers complained to Martha Graham about Ordman. The relationship with Graham ends along with the money, eleven years after Christmas Eve 1964. Batsheva is left holding a name it cannot change, a repertory it may no longer perform, and the Israeli choreographers it will now have to go and find. The funding all goes to Bat-Dor.
suggested_refs: The 1975 rupture between Batsheva de Rothschild and the company bearing her name
sources: Batsheva Dance Company official site, About

stops.name: New York, the Graham works recalled
stops.date_confidence: Manor reports the position of Ron Protas and Linda Hodes as a stated policy following the rupture; he presents it as characterization and the wording may be paraphrase rather than transcript, so the quotation is carried with that flag. No date within the mid-1970s is given, and June 1975 is an ordering anchor
stops.campa: Ron Protas and Linda Hodes, who hold the Graham rights in New York, make the position plain: Graham's works will be seen at Graham's company and nowhere else. The seven pieces handed over in 1964 go home. The first company outside New York ever licensed to dance the repertory is the first to lose the licence, and it loses it for reasons that have nothing to do with dancing. Critics find Batsheva technically strong in the years that follow, and short of anything new.
stops.quote: if you wish to see Graham works performed, you'll have to come to us.
stops.quote_source: Ron Protas and Linda Hodes, as characterized by Giora Manor, Machol Akhshav (Dance Today) no. 27, December 2014, p. 64; possibly paraphrase rather than exact transcript
suggested_refs: The withdrawal of Martha Graham performance rights from Batsheva after 1975
sources: Giora Manor, Dance Today no. 27 (2014), p. 64

stops.name: Beer-Sheva, the Pilates institute in the Negev
stops.date_confidence: the 1975 Pilates institute at Beer-Sheva is attested by French Wikipedia; earlier notes credited it to English Wikipedia, where it does not appear. No month is given and September is an ordering anchor placing it after the Batsheva rupture
stops.campa: In the same year she withdraws from Batsheva she creates a Pilates institute in Beer-Sheva, capital of the Negev and nobody's idea of a dance city. The method is Joseph Pilates's, worked out on spring-and-carriage machines in a boxers' gymnasium on Eighth Avenue in New York, where Graham's injured dancers and Balanchine's were rebuilt in the same room during the years she was paying for one of the two companies. She is sixty, and still moving the same milieu across the same water.
suggested_refs: The Pilates institute at Beer-Sheva, founded 1975

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the centre for dance therapy
stops.date_confidence: the 1985 founding of the Israeli Center for Dance Therapy is attested by French Wikipedia; earlier notes credited it to English Wikipedia, where it does not appear. GAP: no source gives the city, and the Tel Aviv pin is a default for want of one
stops.campa: She founds the Israeli Center for Dance Therapy. Movement is put to work on people who are not dancers and will never perform. She is seventy, and has been paying for dance in this country since the Jerusalem summer course twenty-seven years ago. The foundation carrying her name has been buying music libraries and paying for translations of ancient Hebrew texts since 1962. Her own degree was in biology, taken at the Sorbonne half a century before any of this.

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Israel Prize
stops.date_confidence: the 1989 award is attested by English and French Wikipedia; the ceremony venue and date within the year are not given. The wording widely quoted as the official citation is secondary-site paraphrase, since the Israel government gazette was not fetched in this pass
stops.campa: The state gives her the Israel Prize for special contribution to society and the State of Israel, its highest civil honour, to a woman born in London to a French banking family who has spent thirty-eight years building the country's dance and music infrastructure out of her own inheritance. She is seventy-four. Of the two companies she founded, one is flourishing without her and one is entirely dependent on her, and the prize does not distinguish between them.

stops.name: Neve Tzedek, Tel Aviv: the Suzanne Dellal Centre opens
stops.date_confidence: the centre was established in 1989 and became Batsheva's home; the 2010 Israel Prize and its citation are attested by English Wikipedia. No month is given for the opening. COORDINATES CORRECTED to 32.0608, 34.7642; two earlier notes carried two different wrong points, one of them outside Neve Tzedek
stops.campa: In the oldest Jewish quarter of Tel Aviv, in a compound of restored school buildings around a courtyard, the Suzanne Dellal Centre opens and becomes the home stage of the Batsheva Dance Company. The company she stopped paying for fourteen years earlier acquires the permanent house she never built for it. She is alive, in the same city, funding the other one. In 2010 the centre will take an Israel Prize of its own, for having uplifted the art of dance in Israel.
suggested_refs: The Suzanne Dellal Centre for Dance and Theatre, Neve Tzedek, from 1989

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Ohad Naharin takes the company
stops.date_confidence: the 1990 appointment is attested by English Wikipedia; no month is given. The pin is inherited from martha_graham.journey.json, where the founding of the same company stands
stops.campa: Ohad Naharin becomes artistic director of Batsheva, a quarter century after its founding and fifteen years after its founder walked away from it. He rebuilds the company and develops Gaga, a movement language taught by sensation rather than by shape, which travels out of Tel Aviv to companies and studios across the world. A dance culture imported whole from New York in 1964, on a Rothschild endowment, begins exporting a vocabulary of its own. She is seventy-five and funding Bat-Dor.
suggested_refs: Ohad Naharin and the Gaga movement language, from 1990

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the death at home
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English and French Wikipedia, which give death at her Tel Aviv home after a lengthy illness, aged 84
stops.campa: Batsheva de Rothschild dies at her home in Tel Aviv on the twentieth of April, eighty-four years old, after a long illness. She has lived in the country for thirty-seven years and kept the name it gave her. Of the two companies she founded, the one she abandoned is at the height of its international reputation, and the one she sustained has no income that does not come from her estate. She leaves no children. She leaves a collection of pictures in Europe and a repertory in Israel.
suggested_refs: Obituaries of Batsheva de Rothschild, April 1999, not located in this pass

stops.name: Yarkon Cemetery, Petah Tikva: the grave
stops.date_confidence: burial at the Yarkon cemetery is attested by French Wikipedia and by the English Wikipedia burial category; the day of the funeral is not recorded and 22 April is an anchor two days after the death. COORDINATES CORRECTED to 32.1156, 34.8700, the cemetery's own point; one earlier lens carried a value 3.2 km off. GAP: no plot, marker, photograph or epitaph has been located
stops.campa: She is buried at the Yarkon cemetery outside Tel Aviv, a secular civil ground serving the metropolitan area, among Israeli artists and public figures. There is a family vault in France. She is not in it. Her brother Guy stayed with the bank in Paris; her sister Jacqueline stayed in Los Angeles with a cellist and a chessboard and lived to a hundred. The great-granddaughter of James Mayer de Rothschild lies in a municipal cemetery in the one country of the family's charity she came to live in.
suggested_refs: Yarkon Cemetery, Petah Tikva, and its section registers

stops.campa: The pictures and objects that came down from her grandfather Alphonse are sold in King Street under sale number 6407. Rembrandt's Portrait of a Lady goes to the dealer Robert Noortman for 28.7 million dollars. A thirteenth-century Mamluk jug makes 3,307,750 pounds, a world record for Islamic glass, and two mosque lamps follow it. In Frankfurt the other branch of the house gave its Johann Tischbein portrait to the Städel. This branch sells, in the city where she was born.

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Bat-Dor closes
stops.date_confidence: July 2006 is attested by English Wikipedia for the closure of the Bat-Dor Dance Company after the loss of its principal funding; no day is given
stops.campa: Seven years after her death the Bat-Dor Dance Company stops. It has no second patron and none was ever arranged. Jeannette Ordman's company, funded without a break from 1968, ends in July; Batsheva, cut off in 1975, is by then touring the world with Gaga, rehearsing at the Suzanne Dellal Centre in Neve Tzedek and still carrying the name of the woman who stopped paying for it. What she withdrew from outlived her. What she paid for to the last day did not.
suggested_refs: The closure of the Bat-Dor Dance Company, July 2006
